Volume 11 · Chapter 03

Credit analysis and lending decisions

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v11-c02

By the endEvaluate creditworthiness using cash flow, incentives and downside protection.

Decide whether the borrower can pay, and on what terms

Capability. Build and challenge a credit recommendation from dated operating cash, a funded loan schedule, explicit covenant definitions and a recovery waterfall. Distinguish repayment capacity from accounting profit, project value, collateral value and a lender's expected payoff. The immediate prerequisite is bank balance sheets, capital and liquidity; we also use the accounting and valuation tools of Volumes 7–8 and dated credit cash flows.

Morrow Components wants a bank to lend 120 CU toward a 130 CU plant purchase. Its sponsor offers 20 CU, leaving 10 CU operating cash. Management presents positive earnings, a positive project valuation and an equipment appraisal. None answers the first credit question: what cash will reach the lender on each promised date? This chapter follows the application through refusal of the requested terms, a smaller proposed loan, a downside liquidity test, a delayed collateral recovery and a documented conditional recommendation.

All amounts, businesses, scenarios, probabilities and thresholds are original synthetic teaching assumptions. CU is an arbitrary currency unit, and time is measured in years. No current borrower, market observation, legal priority rule or regulatory minimum is supplied. A numerical pass supports a limited classroom decision; an actual commitment requires verified information and competent authority.

1. Name the primary repayment source before valuing security

Primary repayment is the cash mechanism expected to service the loan in ordinary operation. For this term loan it is operating cash after taxes, maintenance investment and working-capital needs. A seasonal inventory facility might instead revolve as specified inventory is sold and customers pay. A refinancing assumption is a future financing transaction, not cash already committed. A guarantee adds a claim on another party whose capacity, correlation with the borrower and payment timing must themselves be assessed.

Collateral is a potential secondary recovery source. A borrower can have assets worth more than its debt yet miss an earlier payment because those assets cannot be realized in time. An enterprise valuation can support a commercial rationale without demonstrating loan repayment at the chosen dates. A lender normally receives the contractual debt payoff, not all upside in the project. Keeping these objects separate is the first defense against an impressive but irrelevant valuation.

The historical US OCC Commercial Loans booklet provides narrow methodological context: examine financial statements and commitments, connect the repayment schedule to operating cash, and challenge collateral realizability and documentation. Its cover dates the narrative to March 1990 and procedures to March 1998, with a March 2025 removal notice. We use those methods, not its historical thresholds, legal references or assertions about contemporary banking practice.

For each material claim, ask for a reconciliation and a way it could fail. Sales growth needs customer concentration, order quality, collection history and capacity evidence. Receivables need aging, disputes, offsets and related-party checks. Maintenance capex cannot be set to zero merely to improve coverage. Sponsor support requires evidence of funds, competing obligations and timing. A forecast supplied by management is a hypothesis, not an independently measured probability distribution.

2. Build a cash bridge and a fully funded debt schedule

Here EBITDA means the stipulated operating earnings measure before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization. It is neither cash in a bank account nor a universally standardized covenant definition. Define cash available for debt service, before interest and principal, by

CFADSt = EBITDAt − cash taxest − maintenance capext − increase in operating working capitalt.

A working-capital increase consumes cash; a release has a negative sign and adds cash. No dividends, acquisitions, new borrowing or asset-sale proceeds are hidden in this bridge. Expenses already deducted in EBITDA must not be deducted twice. Reconcile cash taxes to the income statement when tax expense differs, and add other genuinely relevant cash items explicitly. The lab's illustrative earnings calculation assumes tax expense equals cash tax and annual depreciation is 15 CU; it makes no claim about actual tax law.

Let L be the initial advance, at scheduled principal, Bt−1 principal outstanding before year t, and r the annual simple coupon on that opening balance. Interest and principal are paid together at year end, after that year's operating cash arrives. Thus B0=L, Bt=Bt−1−at, interest It=rBt−1, and debt service St=It+at. Here all at≥0, their sum is L and every St>0. There is no automatic capitalization of unpaid interest.

Debt-service coverage ratio is DSCRt=CFADSt/St. State the numerator, payment period, debt included and treatment of leases, distributions, extraordinary receipts and revolving debt before comparing ratios. Our borrower has no other scheduled interest-bearing debt; the later default branch separately assumes a prior-ranking workout claim. With a required ratio m, cash headroom is CFADSt−mSt. The ratio has no currency units; headroom is in CU. A zero denominator needs its own interpretation, not an invented infinite number. The bounded lab requires positive service in each year.

Worked example 1 — Profitable operations cannot service the requested loan

Morrow's base operating bridge and requested debt service, CU
YearEBITDACash taxMaintenanceWorking-capital increaseCFADSInterestPrincipalDSCR
16068640124040/52 = 10/13
2627854284042/48 = 7/8
3648844444044/44 = 1

At inception, 120 loan + 20 sponsor cash = 130 plant + 10 cash. The year-1 illustrative net income is 60−15−12−6=27 CU, but total service is 52. Cash available even after consuming the entire opening balance is only 10+40=50. The first payment is short by 2 CU. Contractual full-payment projections would end the three years at (−2,−8,−8); those negative numbers expose missing finance. They do not record an authorized overdraft or prove that later payments occurred after the first failure.

For a separate illustrative enterprise calculation, distribute base CFADS annually, value the operating business at 80 at year 3 and release the required 10 cash then. At a stipulated 10% annual valuation hurdle, project PV is 40/1.1+42/1.1²+(44+80+10)/1.1³ = 171.750563486, against initial uses 140, giving NPV 31.750563486. That assumption-conditioned positive NPV does not put year-3 sale proceeds into the year-1 payment account. The terminal 80 is excluded from our operating repayment schedule and from the separate liquidation branch.

3. Coverage is a flow test; payment feasibility is a dated cash test

Let C0 be loan proceeds plus sponsor cash minus the capital purchase. Assuming those sources are actually received, operating cash earns zero interest here and is retained unless used for service. The full-contract projection is Ct=Ct−1+CFADSt−St. A positive DSCR in one year cannot cure missing initial financing. Conversely, DSCR below one does not by itself imply a missed payment when previously accumulated unrestricted cash is available.

Dated feasibility proposition. For this fixed plan, no extra financing, and a nonnegative required cash floor c, all specified payment dates preserve that floor exactly when

C0 + Σj=1…t(CFADSj−Sj) ≥ c for every t=0,1,2,3.

Proof. Repeated substitution in the cash recursion gives the displayed cumulative balance. If each balance is at least c≥0, every payment can be made and the remaining cash meets the floor, by induction from the funded opening account. If the inequality fails, that date's prescribed service and minimum balance cannot both be financed from the declared sources. An initial injection x shifts every projected balance by x without changing interest or the loan schedule. Therefore the smallest such injection is x*=max(0,c−min0≤t≤3Ct). Choosing x* satisfies all inequalities, and any smaller amount fails at a minimizing date. This proves only the specified annual-date claim. A payroll outflow before customer collections, intra-year seasonality, dividend or restricted account requires a finer dated ledger.

Worked example 2 — A genuine restructure and its remaining covenant risk

Reduce the bank advance to 80, increase sponsor cash to 60, retain the same 130 purchase and 10 opening cash, and charge 8% on opening principal. Principal payments are (20,30,30), so balances before service are (80,60,30), interest (6.4,4.8,2.4) and service (26.4,34.8,32.4). Base DSCRs are (50/33,35/29,110/81)≈(1.515152,1.206897,1.358025). Against a 1.2 floor, cash headrooms are (8.32,.24,5.12). Year 2 is the tight base coverage test, even though it is not the largest outstanding loan balance.

Revised full-service cash projection, with no distributions or cash interest
ScenarioCFADS years 1–3Closing cash years 1–3Extra initial cash needed to preserve 10
Base40,42,4423.6,30.8,42.40
Downturn30,34,3813.6,12.8,18.40

The downside reduces EBITDA to (50,54,58), holding the other stated cash inputs fixed. Its year-2 DSCR is 34/34.8=85/87<1, but 13.6 opening cash plus 34 operating cash funds 34.8 service and leaves 12.8. Retained cash covers the 0.8 flow deficit. By contrast, the requested loan's downside projections are (−12,−26,−32), requiring 42 CU additional initial cash merely to preserve 10 at all three dates.

Restructuring requires a real change in sources as well as amortization. Reducing the loan to 80 while leaving sponsor cash at 20 produces 80+20−130=−30 cash at closing and a 40 gap to the required 10. The program recomputes this gap; it never carries over the old 10 automatically. A sponsor promise without verified, transferable funds does not close it.

4. Use leverage and covenants to create an actionable warning

We define initial gross leverage as this loan's advance divided by base year-1 EBITDA. It is 120/60=2 on the request and 80/60=4/3 on the revision. An assumed internal limit of 1.5 rejects the first and permits the second. Neither this multiple nor debt/equity measures cash available at a particular date. If EBITDA is zero or negative, the lab reports no meaningful positive-earnings multiple and fails this gate, rather than interpreting a negative quotient as exceptionally low leverage.

A covenant must specify the actual parties, calculation, reporting dates, information, threshold and consequences. In our proposed teaching contract, year-end CFADS divided by this loan's scheduled cash interest plus principal must be at least 1.2; operating cash after service must be at least 10; additional debt and distributions need lender consent. Definitions exclude projected sale values and unverified EBITDA add-backs. A ratio based on a three-year average would be a different test and could hide a dated problem.

Origination requires the base forecast to meet 1.2. The supplied downturn has ratios below 1.2 in every year, although its payments and cash floor remain feasible. That is an explicit covenant warning, not a prediction that the loan has already defaulted. The cash projection assumes contractual scheduled payments continue; it does not model acceleration, waiver or enforcement. If the downturn materializes, the proposed process requires updated forecasts and a documented lender decision before any waiver or amended schedule. An automatic waiver would remove the promised control. An automatic acceleration could make this cash projection irrelevant and must be modeled as a changed contract.

Separate an information covenant, such as delivering monthly cash and receivable reports, from a financial maintenance test and from an action restriction. Set an owner and review date. Reconcile actual collections and capex against forecast, track a short-horizon cash forecast, and escalate new liens, missed reports, lost major customers and covenant breaches. More paperwork is not the objective: the information should arrive early enough to change a lending or workout decision.

5. Recoverable cash depends on eligibility, priority and time

A collateral appraisal is not a payout. In a stipulated liquidation, let asset i have reference gross amount Vi, eligible fraction ei and cash realization fraction hi. Gross realized cash is G=ΣVieihi. Deduct specified workout costs W up to G, then a prior-ranking claim H up to the remainder. Cash available to this lender and juniors is A=max(0,G−W−H). For this lender's claim D, its receipt is R=min(D,A), with junior residual A−R. Unpaid higher-ranking costs or claims remain unpaid; they do not become negative lender receipts.

Waterfall check. Partition G sequentially into costs paid, prior claim paid, this lender's receipt and junior residual. Each amount is nonnegative and their sum is G. The lender cannot receive more than either its claim or the remaining estate. Changing a senior claim may affect lender recovery even when the appraisal is unchanged. These are the stipulated contractual priorities of the example, not a general statement of insolvency law. Actual enforceability, competing liens, offsets and legal costs require jurisdiction-specific evidence.

At a declared default immediately before year d's payment, assume all earlier instalments were paid. Our claim is opening principal plus the current year's accrued interest; future unearned coupons are excluded, and no additional default interest is assumed. Recovery arrives at d+ℓ. Under an explicitly chosen annual assessment rate a≥0, its amount discounted to default is R/(1+a)ℓ. Claim shortfall D−R differs from the timing-adjusted comparison D−R/(1+a)ℓ. Neither is cash supplied on the default date by a future sale.

Worked example 3 — A 90 CU equipment reference does not repay a 64.8 CU claim

For the revised loan, stipulate default immediately before the year-2 payment. The remaining principal is 60 and current interest 4.8, so the claim is 64.8. There is no other available estate cash in this branch; operations stop, and neither later CFADS nor the illustrative 80 going-concern terminal value is added to liquidation receipts. The equipment realizes 90×1×.6=54. Receivables with gross amount 40, 75% eligibility and 80% realization contribute 24. From gross cash 78, pay workout cost 8 and a stipulated prior claim 15, leaving 55 for this lender and zero for juniors.

Nominal claim loss is 9.8, with recovery fraction 55/64.8=275/324≈84.876543%. Recovery arrives at year 3. At a stipulated 6% assessment rate, its default-date comparison amount is 55/1.06=2750/53≈51.886792453, so the timing-adjusted shortfall is 12.913207547. The borrower still failed at year 2; the delayed 55 is not a timely instalment or a credit line for the lender.

To illustrate physical scenario analysis, stipulate a 12% chance of exactly this default branch and 88% of full contractual payment. This is a separate two-state experiment, not probabilities estimated from the unweighted base/downturn table. At 6%, promised receipt PV is 83.081201260; default-branch receipt PV is 26.4/1.06+55/1.06³=71.084720944. Weighted receipt PV is .88(83.081201260)+.12(71.084720944)=81.641623622, exceeding the 80 advance by 1.641623622. The calculation omits any separately charged origination, servicing or capital costs; they would reduce this margin. It is a chosen-hurdle scenario comparison, not a Q price, an accounting fair value or demonstrated compensation for all risk.

For fixed branch payoffs, the weighted margin is affine in the stipulated default weight p: M(p)=PVfull−L−p(PVfull−PVdefault). When the default branch is worth less, higher p lowers this margin at a rate equal to the branch PV gap. That derivative is conditional on the payoffs, timing and hurdle staying fixed; deterioration can worsen recovery and funding as well as p. A scenario with acceptable repayment coverage can still be unattractive at the lender's required terms.

6. Underwrite choices and incentives, not just a forecast table

Screening before lending concerns information about the borrower and use of funds. Monitoring after lending concerns new information and behavior. Limited liability, collateral substitution, dividend extraction, hidden liens and origination compensation can separate the borrower's or officer's preference from the lender's. A covenant is useful only if the relevant behavior is observable in time and the promised response is credible. Requiring more equity changes exposure, but does not by itself verify the source of that equity or eliminate every conflict.

Worked example 4 — More project risk can benefit equity and harm the bank

Consider an original one-period alternative use of Morrow's assets, isolated from its three-year cash table. A prudent action pays a certain 120; a gamble pays 200 with probability 1/2 and zero otherwise. Ignore discounting and costs for this comparison. With debt face 100, prudent lender/equity payoffs are (100,20). Under the gamble their expected payoffs are (50,50). The total expected asset payoff falls from 120 to 100, yet equity gains 30 while the lender loses 50. The shareholder can prefer a value-reducing change because upside and downside are allocated differently.

For a debt face F in [0,120], prudent expected equity is 120−F and gamble equity is (200−F)/2. The gamble-minus-prudent difference is F/2−20: gambling is preferred when F>40, the owner is indifferent at 40, and prefers prudence below 40. This is a complete result for these two actions and payoffs, not a general optimal-capital-structure theorem.

Separately, suppose monitoring costs an officer 1 CU of effort, reduces default probability from .15 to .05, and avoids a lender loss of 40 in default. The lender's expected gross credit-loss reduction is (.15−.05)40=4. Subtracting the officer's effort cost gives a 3 improvement in their combined surplus before compensation or penalty transfers; it is not automatically the lender's net income. An officer paid the same immediate origination fee regardless of later outcomes receives no marginal private benefit and avoids the effort. A fully collectible deferred default penalty k creates private expected benefit .10k; monitoring is weakly incentive-compatible when k≥10, and strictly preferred at k=12. This elementary design assumes the officer's action changes those probabilities and the penalty is observable and enforceable; limited liability, correlated shocks and incentives to conceal losses can invalidate it.

7. Write the decision with conditions, evidence and a refusal route

The teaching lab reports six conjunctive gates for each proposal: initial declared sources cover the plant and minimum cash; base DSCR meets 1.2 each year; initial debt/base EBITDA is at most 1.5; all supplied annual cash projections preserve 10; the stated physical-scenario receipt PV minus advance meets an assumed zero margin floor; and sponsor funds, cash forecasts and priority evidence are recorded as verified. Thresholds are inclusive and author-designed. The expected-margin gate is conditional on the chosen probabilities, hurdle and excluded costs; it is not a substitute for a full lending return assessment.

Requested terms: restructure or refuse. The 120 loan fails base DSCR, leverage and the dated cash test. Its positive enterprise NPV and positive assumed lender scenario margin do not cure those failures. Do not approve it by relabeling capex, omitting working-capital needs, or projecting a fresh refinancing transaction without a commitment.

Revised terms: hold for evidence. The 80 loan with 60 sponsor cash passes the five numerical gates under the supplied assumptions, but sponsor funding and collateral priority are not yet verified. The program returns hold_for_evidence. A coherent conditional memo requires the additional sponsor cash actually received before closing, independent cash-forecast checks, confirmation of the assumed priority/recovery rights, and a written covenant-monitoring and escalation process. The downturn covenant breaches need a credible response plan; this analysis grants no advance waiver. If the sponsor cannot fund 60, refuse or redesign the capital purchase and rerun the whole cash model. If the evidence is documented, the output becomes eligible_for_credit_committee_review, not an irrevocable approval.

The reviewer should identify what information could change the decision: a lost customer, slower collections, unavoidable capex, a larger prior claim, a delayed recovery, higher coupon, adverse probability assessment or missing equity. Record who checks each claim and when reconsideration occurs. A lower rate or longer maturity can change cash capacity, but shifts value and exposure rather than manufacturing a free solution. A balloon can reduce early service while concentrating dependence on retained cash, asset realization or refinancing later.

8. Reproduce and challenge the complete credit file

Download the original inputs, standalone Python implementation, complete output, four-payload manifest and contract and reproduction guide. Financial inputs and outputs are exact rational strings. The bounded program needs only the Python standard library; run(data) is quiet and leaves its input unchanged. Explicit checks remain active under optimized Python. The CLI rejects duplicate keys, nonfinite constants, malformed values and unsupported schedules.

Independently reconstruct cash from cumulative receipts minus cumulative interest and principal, rather than copying the program's bank loop. Check the waterfall with conservation and cap identities, and reconstruct every default/survival payment date before discounting. Perturb sponsor cash separately from the loan, working-capital timing separately from EBITDA, and recovery delay separately from sale proceeds. These checks can establish arithmetic against declared assumptions. They cannot authenticate documents, estimate a physical law or guarantee all-path repayment. The year-end cash test also leaves intra-year liquidity unresolved.

Exercises

  1. Profit and service. Reconstruct year-1 CFADS and net income under each loan. Give requested and revised year-1 closing cash and DSCR. Explain why depreciation is treated differently in the two bridges and why principal is not an income-statement expense.
  2. A liquidity boundary and proof. For the revised downturn, increase only year-2 working-capital investment by x≥0. Derive all affected closing balances and the largest x that preserves 10 without new financing. Evaluate x=2.8 and x=2.80000001. Prove the minimum initial-injection formula for any finite fixed schedule under this chapter's assumptions.
  3. Sources must follow the restructure. Change the loan from 120 to 80 and its payments to the revised schedule, but keep sponsor cash at 20. Compute opening cash and the gap to the 10 floor. Why do improved debt-service ratios not solve this defect? If instead the original 120 loan is retained, how much additional initial cash does each supplied scenario need to maintain 10?
  4. A balloon is a changed cash plan. Keep the revised 80 advance, 60 sponsor cash and 8% coupon, but pay all principal at year 3. Compute service, base DSCRs and the three base closing cash balances. Can the borrower make these payments under the stated retention policy? Does it pass the 1.2 base coverage gate? Identify two assumptions that would make the apparent cash comfort unreliable.
  5. Seniority and delay. In the revised default branch, raise only the prior claim to 25 and the recovery delay to two years. Recompute gross sale proceeds, this lender's nominal recovery and claim loss, recovery year, default-date discounted recovery at 6%, and timing-adjusted shortfall. Then set the prior claim to 100: what pays, and how is gross cash conserved?
  6. Physical probability is not a pricing law. Hold the revised two branch cash flows and 6% assessment rate fixed. Derive the largest default weight p for which discounted expected receipts cover the 80 advance. Evaluate p=.30. Separately retain p=.12 but use an 8% assessment rate.   7. Incentive compatibility. Reconstruct lender and equity expected payoffs for the prudent action and gamble at debt faces 20,40 and100. Prove the threshold F=40 for 0≤F≤120.   8. Underwriting memo and model critique. Write a 300-word recommendation covering both proposals, the two missing verification items, covenant handling, a dated cash limitation and the meaning of the collateral/scenario margin. Specify one new intervention with a predicted direction and one observation that would trigger refusal or redesign. Explain why changing a forecast solely to make a gate pass is inadequate evidence.

    Rubric,10 points. Award2 for correct proposal-specific cash/rate/leverage conclusions;2 for source verification and an actual funding condition;2 for covenant rights plus an intra-year limitation;2 for recovery timing and probability/discount scope;2 for a correctly traced intervention and an actionable refusal trigger. Different defensible policies earn full credit with reconciled numbers and explicit assumptions. A spreadsheet plug, silently omitted cash use, assumed waiver or claim of actual approval requires correction regardless of total. Forecast revision needs new evidence or a changed economic contract; passing a gate is not such evidence.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. In two minutes explain how a borrower can have positive NPV and earnings, fail one loan, and service another in a year with DSCR below one. Then explain why collateral can reduce the lender's eventual loss without funding the missed payment. Answer standard: identify different objects and dates; reproduce requested year-1 service52 versus cash50, revised downside year-2 service34.8 versus cash47.6, and delayed recovery55. Name retained unrestricted cash as the bridge in the second case, not an assumed new loan. Explain why the downside's1.2 covenant warning still requires action.

Find the two closing balances and smallest initial injection. Separately a lender claim30 has gross collateral25, costs3, a prior claim7 and recovery after one year at a5% assessment rate. Find nominal recovery and discounted shortfall. Answers: cash closes at9 then5, so no injection is needed despite second-year DSCR2/3. Recovery ismin(30,25−3−7)=15; nominal loss15 and discounted shortfall30−15/1.05=110/7≈15.714286. Explain why these dated cash tests do not identify a default probability.

Sources and further study

The historical OCC booklet is used within the stated repayment/documentation/collateral scope. The cash-feasibility proof, Morrow case, priority waterfall, finite incentive examples, problems and code are original. The chapter does not cover every real loan agreement, restructuring process or insolvency jurisdiction. Continue to market risk and portfolio loss for distributional loss measures; a measure built on a missing cash use or an unsupported scenario law cannot repair this underwriting file.

Sources and further study

  • OCC, Comptroller's Handbook — Commercial Loans (Section 206): narrative March 1990, procedures March 1998 — Historical US methodological context for borrower financial/cash analysis, primary repayment sources, term-loan amortization, collateral realizability and documented monitoring. Original case, thresholds, priority assumptions and proofs are not attributed to the source.
